planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+), at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis, since Greasy Bean is a vigorous climber needing 6–8 feet of support.

directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young for snap beans or let pods mature for a rich, flavorful shelly or dry bean. Greasy Bean is a distinctive category of heirloom Appalachian pole bean named for the unusual smooth, glossy, almost oil-slicked appearance of the pods, which lack the fuzzy surface texture of most common beans — a trait that has made these beans prized heirlooms passed down through generations of mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, and West Virginia, with many distinct named strains maintained within individual families. The tender, stringless pods have excellent flavor as snap beans when young, and the plump, flavorful seeds shell out well for cooking as a traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous, productive vines reward a sturdy support and reliable moisture through the growing season. A true regional heirloom treasure for gardeners interested in Appalachian foodways, zone 4–10.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+); traditionally interplanted at the base of standing corn stalks, which the vigorous climbing vines use as a living pole in the old 'three sisters' style of companion planting.

directions: Sow at the base of standing corn or a sturdy pole in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a true climbing type, it needs tall support to perform well. Genuine Cornfield Bean is an old-time American heirloom pole bean, so named because it was traditionally grown climbing up living corn stalks in the cornfield rather than on a dedicated trellis — a direct descendant of the indigenous 'three sisters' companion-planting tradition of interplanting corn, beans, and squash, in which the bean's nitrogen-fixing roots benefit the heavy-feeding corn while the cornstalk provides the bean a ready-made climbing pole. The vigorous vines produce a heavy crop of medium green pods good for snap use when young, or left to mature and dry for a flavorful winter soup bean. A practical, space-efficient heirloom for gardeners who want to grow beans and corn together in the traditional way, zone 4–10.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile soil in full sun, after all frost danger has passed. Allow the full season to dry down on the stalk for grinding into meal or distilling.

directions: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; let ears fully dry on the stalk for the deepest color and best grinding or distilling quality. Jimmy Red is a South Carolina heirloom dent corn with a dramatic history — the variety nearly vanished entirely, surviving through only a handful of ears kept by a single South Carolina farming family, before being rediscovered and reintroduced in the 2010s by chef and miller Glenn Roberts of Anson Mills and distiller Scott Blackwell, who used it to help revive heirloom Southern corn whiskey and grits production. The deep garnet-red, almost purple-black kernels grind into a rich, distinctively flavored meal and grits, and the variety has become especially prized by craft distillers for producing bourbon and moonshine with a uniquely deep, earthy character credited to the corn's high oil content and pigmentation. A striking, historically significant heirloom for gardeners interested in Southern foodways and heritage grain, zone 6–10.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+), at the base of a sturdy 6–8 foot pole or trellis, since Speckled Cutshort is a vigorous heirloom climber.

directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods young and tender for snap use, or let mature for a flavorful dry soup bean. Speckled Cutshort is a member of the Appalachian 'cutshort' family of heirloom pole beans, so named for the short, blunt, somewhat flattened pod tip characteristic of the type, and passed down for generations among mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, and the Carolinas, with many named strains maintained within individual families and communities. The pods are speckled with purple-brown markings while developing, turning fully green as they mature, and the tender, meaty texture makes them excellent as a snap bean; left to dry, the attractively speckled seeds cook into a rich, traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous and productive on a sturdy support, it is a genuine piece of living Appalachian food heritage for gardeners who want an authentic regional heirloom, zone 4–10.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile soil in full sun, after all frost danger has passed; allow ears to fully dry down on the stalk before harvest for grinding into meal.

directions: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and well adapted to the heat of a long Texas or Gulf South growing season. Texas Gourdseed is an old Southern dent corn named for the distinctive deep, thin, wedge-shaped indentation at the crown of each dried kernel, resembling the shape of a small gourd seed — a hallmark trait of the historic 'Gourdseed' corn family that was among the most widely grown field corns across the antebellum and postbellum South before hybrid corn displaced open-pollinated varieties in the 20th century. The tall, vigorous stalks are well adapted to hot, humid Southern summers and produce a reliable grain crop even under the drought stress that limits many other corns, grinding into a flavorful, traditional cornmeal and grits. A genuine piece of Southern agricultural history for gardeners interested in growing and preserving heritage field corn, zone 6–10.
